A convent is a place where a group of nuns live together as a religious community. It refers to two closely connected things at once:

  1. The building (or complex of buildings) where nuns live
  2. The community of nuns living there

So when someone says "she entered the convent," they mean she became a nun and joined that religious community. When someone says "the convent is on the hill," they're talking about the physical building.

Nuns — women who have chosen to dedicate their entire lives to God and religious service. To become a nun, a woman takes formal vows, which are solemn, binding religious promises. These typically include:

  • Poverty — giving up personal wealth and ownership
  • Chastity — choosing a life without romantic or sexual relationships
  • Obedience — following the rules of their religious order and their superiors

Once a woman takes these vows, she becomes a full member of the convent's community. The nuns in a convent belong to a particular religious order — an organized group within the Catholic Church (or sometimes other Christian denominations) that follows a specific set of rules and traditions. Examples include the Carmelites, the Poor Clares, the Dominicans, and the Sisters of Charity.

The head or leader of a convent is usually called a Mother Superior or an Abbess, who is responsible for guiding and governing the community.
What goes on inside a convent?

Life in a convent is highly structured and revolves around two main pillars: prayer and work.

The nuns follow a daily rhythm that includes multiple sessions of communal prayer at fixed times throughout the day — early morning, midday, evening, and sometimes during the night. This practice of praying together at set hours is called the Divine Office or the Liturgy of the Hours, and it forms the backbone of convent life.

Outside of prayer, nuns also work. The nature of this work depends on the type of convent.

1. Enclosed (or cloistered) convents

In these convents, the nuns live in almost complete separation from the outside world. They rarely, if ever, leave the convent premises. Their primary purpose is contemplation — deep, devoted prayer and meditation. They believe their life of prayer benefits the world spiritually, even without going out into it. The Poor Clares and the Discalced Carmelites are well-known examples of enclosed orders.

In a cloistered convent, there is often a grille — a partition or screen — between the nuns and any visitors, maintaining a physical separation even when they do communicate with outsiders.

2. Active (or apostolic) convents

In these convents, nuns balance prayer with direct service to the wider community. They go out into the world and do practical work such as:

  • Teaching in schools
  • Nursing and caring for the sick
  • Running orphanages or shelters
  • Doing missionary work
  • Social work among the poor

The Missionaries of Charity, founded by Mother Teresa, are a famous example of an active order.
The physical structure of a convent

A convent is not just a single building — it is typically a complex that includes several spaces built to support the community's life:

  • A chapel or oratory — the central space for prayer and worship
  • Cells — small, simple, private rooms where each nun sleeps and sometimes prays alone (not prison cells; the word comes from the Latin for a small room)
  • A refectory — the communal dining hall
  • A cloister — a covered walkway forming a square around an open courtyard, often used for quiet walking and reflection; this is also where the word "cloistered" comes from
  • Gardens, a library, a kitchen, and workrooms

The design is intentional: everything is arranged to support a life of simplicity, prayer, and community.

These words are closely related and often confused:

  • Monastery: Traditionally used for a community of monks (men), though in strict usage it can apply to any enclosed religious community, male or female. In everyday speech, people tend to say "monastery" for men and "convent" for women.
  • Nunnery: An older, more literary or historical term for a convent. You'll encounter it in older literature (Shakespeare uses it), but it's rarely used today.
  • Abbey: A larger, self-governing religious house — it can be for either monks or nuns. A convent may sometimes be called an abbey if it has a certain level of independence and is led by an abbess.
  • Priory: A smaller religious house, often dependent on a larger abbey.
  • Friary: A house for friars (members of mendicant orders like the Franciscans or Dominicans).

The simplest rule: in modern usage, convent = community and home of nuns.

Because many convents historically ran schools, people in some countries (especially in Ireland, India, and parts of the UK) informally use "convent" to refer to a school run by nuns — as in "She studied at a convent" or "It's a convent school." This is a derived, informal usage rather than the core meaning, but it is widely understood and common in everyday speech.

A convent is both the community of nuns and the place where they live. It is a self-contained world built around religious vows, structured prayer, and — depending on the type — either deep contemplative solitude or active service to others. The word captures not just a building, but a whole way of life chosen by women who have committed themselves entirely to their faith.
